questions.q: State Coulomb's Law in vector form for the force on charge \(q_2\) due to \(q_1\). Define every symbol and give the SI value of the proportionality constant \(k\).
questions.a: \(\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}\) where \(\vec{F}_{12}\) is force on \(q_2\) due to \(q_1\) (N), \(q_1, q_2\) are point charges (C), \(r\) is separation (m), \(\hat{r}_{12}\) is unit vector from \(q_1\) to \(q_2\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \ \text{C}^2 \text{N}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2}\), and \(k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0 \approx 9 \times 10^9 \ \text{N m}^2 \text{C}^{-2}\). A wrong answer reveals: missing vector notation (treating force as scalar), confusing \(\hat{r}_{12}\) with \(\hat{r}_{21}\), or using \(k = 9 \times 10^9\) without units.

questions.q: Two charges \(+3 \ \mu\text{C}\) and \(-2 \ \mu\text{C}\) are placed 10 cm apart in vacuum. A student calculates the force magnitude as \(F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{3 \times 2}{10^2} = 5.4 \times 10^9 \ \text{N}\). Identify every error in this calculation.
questions.a: Errors: (1) Charges not converted to coulombs: \(3 \ \mu\text{C} = 3 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{C}\), \(-2 \ \mu\text{C} = -2 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{C}\). (2) Distance not converted to meters: \(10 \ \text{cm} = 0.1 \ \text{m}\). (3) Used \(r = 10\) instead of \(r^2 = 0.01\). (4) Ignored sign of product for direction (though magnitude uses absolute value). Correct: \(F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \frac{|3 \times 10^{-6} \times -2 \times 10^{-6}|}{(0.1)^2} = 5.4 \ \text{N}\) attractive. A wrong answer reveals the student treats μC and cm as SI units — a pervasive unit-conversion error.

questions.q: Calculate the electrostatic force on a charge \(q_1 = +4.0 \ \mu\text{C}\) placed at \(x = 0\) due to \(q_2 = -6.0 \ \mu\text{C}\) at \(x = 30 \ \text{cm}\) on the x-axis. Express the answer in vector form using \(\hat{i}\).
questions.a: Given: \(q_1 = +4.0 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{C}\), \(q_2 = -6.0 \times 10^{-6} \ \text{C}\), \(r = 0.30 \ \text{m}\). \(\hat{r}_{12} = +\hat{i}\) (from \(q_1\) to \(q_2\)). \(\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12} = (9 \times 10^9) \frac{(4.0 \times 10^{-6})(-6.0 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.30)^2} \hat{i} = -2.4 \ \hat{i} \ \text{N}\). The negative sign means force on \(q_1\) is toward \(q_2\) (attraction). A wrong answer reveals: sign error in vector direction, forgetting to square distance, or misplacing \(\hat{i}\) direction.

questions.q: The force between two point charges is \(F\) when they are in vacuum. If the same charges are placed at the same separation in a medium of relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r = 4\), what is the new force? Explain why Coulomb's Law in the form \(F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\) does not directly apply.
questions.a: New force \(F' = F / \varepsilon_r = F/4\). The given formula is strictly for vacuum (or air ≈ vacuum). In a dielectric medium, the permittivity becomes \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0\), so the force reduces by factor \(\varepsilon_r\). Coulomb's Law in matter is \(F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\). A wrong answer reveals the student thinks the formula is universal for all media, missing the role of \(\varepsilon_0\) as "permittivity of free space" specifically.

questions.q: A student claims: "Coulomb's Law proves that the force between two charges is always repulsive because \(k\), \(q_1\), \(q_2\), and \(r^2\) are all positive quantities." Evaluate this statement and correct the misconception.
questions.a: The statement is false. The scalar magnitude formula \(F = k|q_1 q_2|/r^2\) uses absolute values and gives only magnitude. The vector form \(\vec{F}_{12} = k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}\) includes the algebraic signs of \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). If \(q_1 q_2 > 0\) (like charges), \(\vec{F}_{12}\) is along \(\hat{r}_{12}\) (repulsion). If \(q_1 q_2 < 0\) (unlike charges), \(\vec{F}_{12}\) is opposite to \(\hat{r}_{12}\) (attraction). A wrong answer reveals the student confuses the magnitude formula with the vector law and ignores the sign of charge product.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment using only Coulomb's Law and Newton's Third Law to show that the forces \(\vec{F}_{12}\) and \(\vec{F}_{21}\) are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction for any two point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\).
questions.a: From Coulomb's Law: \(\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}\) and \(\vec{F}_{21} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_2 q_1}{r^2} \hat{r}_{21}\). Since \(\hat{r}_{21} = -\hat{r}_{12}\) and multiplication is commutative (\(q_1 q_2 = q_2 q_1\)), we get \(\vec{F}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{12}\). This satisfies Newton's Third Law identically for all \(q_1, q_2, r\). A poor answer reveals the student cannot connect the vector direction reversal (\(\hat{r}_{21} = -\hat{r}_{12}\)) to the action-reaction pair.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Coulomb's Law states that the ______ force between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining the charges.
Fill in the blank: Observe a rubbed plastic ruler attracting tiny paper bits — the force acts at a ______ without contact.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can compute the magnitude and direction of the electrostatic force between two point charges given their magnitudes, signs, and separation in vacuum, correctly handling unit conversions (μC to C, cm to m) and applying the vector form to determine attraction or repulsion.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Observe a rubbed plastic ruler ______ tiny paper bits — the force acts at a distance without contact.
